Source: Lenard Lakofka, “A recipe for the Alchemist,” Leomund's Tiny Hut, Dragon #49 (May 1981), p.56-60. Restated in plain words; the numbers follow the article.

The alchemist is a little-known kind of magic-user, and is always a non-player character. The class is written up so the DM knows what an alchemist can and cannot do when the party meets one in town or hires one as a henchman.

Some ordinary trades are part of alchemy: potter, glassblower, brewer and distiller. So a tradesman the party meets may know a little alchemy. Brewers and distillers don't need to learn magic to work at their trades.

Who can be an alchemist

  • Strength 9 or more, intelligence 10 or more, wisdom 6 or more, dexterity 9 or more, constitution 14 or more, and charisma under 16.
  • Humans, elves and half-elves. Only humans can become Masters and Grandmasters.
  • Never multi-classed.
  • Every alchemist is lawful: 80% lawful neutral, 10% lawful evil, 10% lawful good. A low-level alchemist may have another alignment, but all have turned lawful by 6th level (Identifier).

Intelligence limits

Harder spells and potions need more intelligence, and an alchemist who isn't smart enough can never learn or make them:

  • Intelligence 12: 3rd level spells and second difficulty potions.
  • Intelligence 14: 4th level spells and third difficulty potions.
  • Intelligence 16: 5th level spells and fourth difficulty potions.

Experience

Alchemists earn experience only by working at their trade, never by adventuring. These awards are here in case the DM wants to raise a non-player novice a few levels so he or she is more useful as a henchman.

  • Each piece of pottery used in the trade: 3 xp (no longer given after 3rd level).
  • Each major glass instrument blown or made: 6 xp (no longer given after 5th level).
  • Each potion identified by the “10% test”: 7 xp (no longer given after 7th level).
  • Each potion made correctly: 10% of the potion's xp value, or 20 xp if it has none. This is given for every good potion.
  • Each poison made correctly: 5 xp mild, 15 toxic, 25 lethal, 40 destructive. Masters and Grandmasters don't get this award.
  • Each mixture analysis done correctly: 45 xp.
  • Each spell learned: 7 xp per level of the spell.

The hit dice also set the alchemist's “magic level”: the level at which spells are cast for range, duration, area of effect and so on. It is the number of dice, not the experience level. A Scholar is 7th level but has 4+6 dice, so casts spells at 4th level. Alchemists go no higher than Grandmaster, 11th level, with a magic level of 7.

There can be several Grandmasters, but rarely near each other. If two live in the same town, one may well try to kill the other.

Fighting, saves and gear

  • An alchemist forced to fight does so as a magic-user. Saving throws are a magic-user's, but 2 worse on every kind except saves vs. spells.
  • Alchemists seldom use weapons, but can learn two: the dagger (never thrown) and the dart. Both may be magical.
  • No magic armor of any kind, bracers of defense included. Protection items (cloaks and rings) are allowed.
  • No rods or staves. The only wands are wands of detection and of magic missiles. Scrolls are useless to an alchemist, even with read magic.
  • From the DMG's miscellaneous magic, an alchemist may own: alchemy jug (a Master can get two kinds of liquid a day from it), bag of transmuting, bag of holding, beaker of plentiful potions, brooch of shielding, crystal ball, decanter of endless water, dust of appearance, dust of disappearance, dust of sneezing and choking, flask of curses, helm of comprehending languages and reading magic, helm of telepathy, Keoghtom's ointment, manual of bodily health, mirror of mental prowess, Nolzur's marvelous pigments, periapt of health, periapt of proof against poison, scarab of protection, stone of good luck, stone of weight, and the iron flask of Tuerny the Merciless.

Alchemese

Alchemists write their “prescriptions” (potion recipes) and their spells in a language of their own, Alchemese.

  • A magic-user needs both read magic and comprehend languages to use an alchemist's spell book. Once a spell is understood, the magic-user doesn't need the two spells to read that spell again.
  • To copy a spell from a magic-user's book into his or her own, an alchemist needs read magic and write. The spell must be translated and then written down; the alchemist can't learn it straight from the magic-user's book and write it out later.
  • Copying without write is possible, but takes a week per spell level and has a 10% chance of error per spell level. An error ruins the spell 80% of the time; the other 20% the spell backfires.
  • Clerics and illusionists can't understand Alchemese, and alchemists can't read their scrolls or books either.

Special notes

Each level from 1st to 9th brings new skills, marked A to I on the alchemists table. What is learned at a lower level still applies higher up unless a later skill replaces it. (A Potter knows no alchemy, but a high-level alchemist hasn't forgotten how to make pots.)

  • A. Potter. Makes the pottery the alchemist uses to heat, stir, grind and store things, and learns to tend the hearth. Each pot is made from scratch and takes at least 48 hours. The chart gives the chance it comes out right; if not, the pot is useless. A Potter knows nothing of alchemy. Pottery sells for 1-100 SP a piece, depending on the item.
  • B. Glassblower. Makes beakers, flasks and other glass for the laboratory, 3-8 hours a piece. Graduates (8th level) and higher always make pottery and glass successfully. Glass sells for 6-600 SP an item. The DM decides how much pottery and glass an experiment needs. Alchemists often keep novices to make these for them. Potters and glassblowers may stay in those trades and never study further.
  • C. Apprentice. Begins to learn minor magic. Every Apprentice is taught read magic, and can learn other spells the way a magic-user does, from Alchemese. The spell list gives the charge for casting a spell, where there is one.
    Apprentices also learn the “10% test”: sipping a tenth of a potion to identify it. It only works on a potion the alchemist has fully learned by testing before, so a list of potions tested is kept for each Apprentice. The alchemist studies how the liquid reacts, not its taste, smell or color, since potions with the same effect may look and taste nothing alike if made by different alchemists (the same alchemist's potions always match). A potion never tested before stays unknown, but adds to what the alchemist knows. A Grandmaster always knows a similar potion by the test if he or she has drunk one before. Apprentices charge 40 GP for the test; 10 GP more per level of the alchemist may be added, since the test gets more accurate at higher levels.
  • D. Brewer. Learns to make compounds by boiling and mixing. A Brewer must be told what to mix, or is 85% likely to fail. First difficulty potions can be tried this way, but a failure makes a potion with the opposite effect:
    • Animal control: the animal flies into a blind rage.
    • Climbing: the climber is pushed away from the surface.
    • Delusion: the drinker becomes more alert and thoughtful, but then gives in to almost any suggestion.
    • Levitation: the figure drops as if twice as heavy, so falling damage is doubled and item saving throws are at −1.
    • Sweet water: fouls the water further, into a mild poison (2d4 damage).
    • Skeleton/zombie control: those monsters attack the drinker and ignore everyone else, and no cleric within 20 feet of the drinker can turn or destroy them.
    • Water breathing: the figure gags and coughs, and drowns twice as fast.
    • Dust of appearance: fails, so invisible things are not revealed.
    None of these failures shows at first, so the Brewer or drinker thinks the potion is good. The 10% test or a normal analysis can find the defect, but at −30% to the usual chance.
    Brewers can make many compounds, but nothing that needs crystallizing or distilling (that is, second difficulty potions and up). A Brewer is 75% likely to know how to brew beer, ale or malt liquor, and may make some for extra money if the master allows such “nonsense.”
  • E. Alember. Studies distilling. Can do steps of potion making, always under direct supervision. Learns the basics of Alchemese. Without comprehend languages, no one else can read an alchemist's prescription. (Magic-users of 11th level can learn Alchemese, and then no longer need an alchemist to make potions.) An Alember can try a potion alone, but it may fail, even with comprehend languages.
  • F. Identifier. Begins 2nd level spells. Identify potion is always taught first, and for the chance to learn it the student counts intelligence as 2 points higher. No new skills.
  • G. Scholar. Learns 3rd level spells and how to make poisons, in four strengths: mild, toxic, lethal and destructive (see Potions and Poisons).
  • H. Graduate. Learns to identify potions by analysis, without drinking them. Analysis uses up 10% of the potion. Without the prescription in the Graduate's book, the chance of naming the potion wrongly is 40%; with it, 15%. Every analysis has a 10% chance of an explosion, checked before seeing whether the analysis worked. That chance drops 2% per level above 8th, so a Grandmaster's lab explodes only 4% of the time. The explosion does 4d4 damage. Charge: 150 GP.
  • I. Alchemist (9th level). Learns what happens when two potions are mixed, and can predict it by analysis with 70% accuracy (Master 80%, Grandmaster 90%). Use the potion mixing chart on DMG p.119. If the accuracy roll succeeds, tell the player the true result; if not, roll on the chart again and tell the player that result instead. Charge: 450 GP.
    The analysis really mixes about 5% of each potion, so the result does happen, on a much smaller scale; an explosion from it does 1d8. The analysis itself can also explode: 20% for an Alchemist, 15% for a Master, 10% for a Grandmaster, for 4d6 damage.
    Two alchemists' versions of the same potion mix the same way only if their prescriptions are identical. A healing potion might explode with a potion of gaseous form, but if either was made from another prescription, mixing them gives a different result.

Potions by difficulty

These are the potions (and a few substances) that can be made from prescriptions in Alchemese. An alchemist can't make potions harder than his or her intelligence allows.

  • First difficulty (intelligence 10+): animal control, climbing, delusion, levitation, sweet water, skeleton/zombie control, water breathing, dust of appearance.
  • Second difficulty (12+): clairaudience, clairvoyance, diminution, fire resistance, healing, oil of slipperiness, philter of love, poison, speed, ghoul/ghast control.
  • Third difficulty (14+): ESP, extra healing, flying, gaseous form, invisibility, longevity, philter of persuasiveness, plant control, polymorph self, wight/wraith/shadow control, dust of disappearance, dust of sneezing & choking.
  • Fourth difficulty (16+): dragon control, heroism, human control, invulnerability, oil of etherealness, super-heroism, treasure finding, ghost/vampire/spectre control, Keoghtom's ointment, Nolzur's marvelous pigments.

Alchemists can start making potions at 4th level, but the chance of getting one wrong is high then. A 5th level alchemist with enough intelligence can even try a fourth difficulty potion, with only a small chance of success.

The article doesn't give recipes. The DMG suggests some key ingredients (p.116-117), and others can be swapped in. Each prescription names its key ingredient. Using a substitute lowers the chance of success by 10% for a first difficulty potion, 16% for second, 23% for third and 40% for fourth.

When a potion fails

The abilities chart gives the chance of making a potion. When the attempt fails, roll percentile dice on this table to see what the potion turned out to be:

Success1-251-15
Complete failure26-4516-50
Explosion (6d4 damage)46-5051-58
Half efficacy51-6059-64
Opposite effect61-7065-79
Mild poison (5d4)71-9080-90
Toxic poison (5d6)91-9691-96
Lethal poison (death unless a save is made; 4d6 in any case)97-0097-00

Modifiers to the roll: an alchemist of 6th level (Identifier) or higher subtracts 23 for each level above 5th. A non-alchemist, or a magic-user under 11th level, subtracts 2 for each level above 1st. A 10th or 11th level alchemist subtracts more than 100, so every potion he or she makes comes out right. A result under 01 counts as 01.

Examples: a Scholar (7th level) reading a prescription subtracts 2 × 23 = 46. A roll of 86 becomes 40: complete failure. An 8th level fighter with a helm of comprehending languages and reading magic subtracts 7 × 2 = 14. The fighter still needs the intelligence for the potion's difficulty, so with intelligence 11 he can't make a second difficulty potion even with the helm. An 8th level magic-user has the same chance as the fighter.

Magic-users and alchemy

Only at 11th level do magic-users gain real alchemist skills. For anything an alchemist does, a magic-user counts as an alchemist of a lower level:

Magic-user levelCounts as alchemist level
11-128
13-149
15-1610
17+11+

So a 14th level magic-user works as a 9th level alchemist. Learning alchemy gives a magic-user no extra spells. A spell written in Alchemese is learned at its alchemist level, whatever its level as a magic-user spell, and works only as an alchemist's would. For example, a 12th level Wizard who wants to learn magic missile in Alchemese must learn it as a 5th level spell, even though he knows it as a 1st level magic-user spell, and gets only four missiles from it, as an alchemist would. That holds even at 20th level. An alchemist's highest effective level for range, duration and so on is 7th.

“Success” to “Half efficacy” are the d100 result of making the poison. A half-efficacy ingested poison does, on a failed save, the damage the full poison does on a successful save; on a successful save it does nothing. A half-efficacy insinuative poison does 2d4, 2d6, 2d10 and 2d12 (types A to D) on a failed save, and nothing on a successful one. These types roughly match the DMG list on p.20, which also gives their costs.

Modifiers to the roll: an alchemist subtracts 16 for each level above 7th. A magic-user subtracts only 8 for each level above 11th, and no more than 40 in all, since magic-users don't make poisons as well as alchemists. The DM may forbid magic-users from making poisons at all.

Business

An alchemist may buy items the party finds, or trade potions for them, or knock something off the price of buying, making or testing a potion.

Alchemists fight poorly and have few useful combat spells, so they seldom go adventuring, even for an important raw material. An alchemist henchman of any level goes on a trip only with plenty of protection and no need to face danger. Henchmen give their bosses a small discount on potions they make, since the boss provides room, board and maybe raw materials.

Alchemists, Masters and Grandmasters like to hire 3-10 helpers or novices for the lab, and would like their patrons to pay for them. Those who have set up shop in a town have hirelings, including guards. That overhead puts their potion and testing prices 40-100% above the list prices.

Each alchemist spell is the same as the magic-user, cleric or druid spell of that name, except that range, duration, area of effect and so on use the alchemist's magic level (hit dice). Magic-users of 11th level and up who learn these spells also use the alchemist equivalent, not their own level. The article marks altered spells * and spells new to alchemists # (magic-users can use the new ones too). Some spells list a charge to a customer for casting them. All are in the Alchemist Spells compendium, where the altered and new spells are written out.

What the module does

  • Adds the class Alchemist (Dragon #49) with its own spell list, Alchemist: the article's titles, experience and spells by level, and hit points by the alchemists table (the dice plus the fixed points). Spells are cast at the magic level.
  • Attacks use the magic-user table; saves are the magic-user's, 2 worse except vs. spells.
  • The Alchemist tab rolls each ability on the chart, the analysis explosion check, mixture analysis, and poisons by type with the level modifier. A familiar can be set to add 5% to every chance, or take 5% off after one is killed.
  • The Record tab shows notes, which never block anything: ability scores out of range, a race or level not allowed, more than one class, an alchemist of 6th level or more who isn't lawful, and magic armor or bracers of defense worn.

Choices made here

  • When a potion roll fails the chart, the module reads the same d100 roll on the failure table with the level modifier. From 5th level up, a “Success” on the table falls exactly within the chart's first difficulty chance, so for a failed roll the table can only show “Success” at 4th level or on a harder potion; the module then reads it as complete failure.
  • Proficiency slots, which the article doesn't give, are the magic-user's, with −5 when not proficient. The article allows only the dagger and the dart.
  • Armor: the article bars magic armor and bracers of defense, and says nothing about ordinary armor, so only magic armor and bracers are noted.
  • Magic missile is printed “(4)”, and the article's example says an alchemist gets four missiles, so the spell always gives four.
  • Shrink is taken as the reverse of enlarge (reduce), so its entry carries the enlarge text. Leomund's trap and Tenser's floating disk use the system's names, false trap and floating disc.
